title: Vehicle dynamics
text:
As a master’s student, you do not need to memorize every derived formula (like the full state-space matrix or the understeer gradient formula). Instead, memorize these fundamental physical and geometric relationships. Every complex model in this course can be derived from these building blocks.


These are the core Newton-Euler equations governing the vehicle’s dynamic behavior in a moving reference frame. Because the frame itself is rotating (yawing), we get Coriolis acceleration terms (the \(v_y\omega_z\) and \(v_x\omega_z\) components).

Longitudinal Equation of Motion: \[m a_x = m(\dot{v}_x - v_y\omega_z) = \sum F_x\] Explanation: Balances the mass times longitudinal acceleration (including the centripetal effect of lateral velocity and yaw) with the sum of all external longitudinal forces.
Lateral Equation of Motion: \[m a_y = m(\dot{v}_y + v_x\omega_z) = \sum F_y\] Explanation: Balances the mass times lateral acceleration with the sum of all external lateral forces. This is your starting point for cornering analysis.
Yaw (Moment about Z-axis): \[I_{zz}\ddot{\psi} = I_{zz}\dot{\omega}_z = \sum M_z\] Explanation: Relates the vehicle’s yaw moment of inertia and yaw angular acceleration to the sum of moments generated by the tires around the center of gravity.
Vertical Equation of Motion (Static/Quasi-static): \[m a_z = F_{z1} + F_{z2} - mg = 0\] Explanation: Assuming no vertical acceleration, the sum of the vertical tire forces must support the vehicle’s weight.
Pitch (Moment about Y-axis): \[I_{yy}\dot{\omega}_y = F_{z2}b - F_{z1}a - (F_{x1} + F_{x2})h = 0\] Explanation: Assuming zero pitch acceleration, this moment balance is crucial for deriving the longitudinal load transfer (how weight shifts during braking or accelerating).





These equations sum the forces and moments specifically for the single-track model. They assume the steering angle \(\delta\) is small enough that \(\cos\delta \approx 1\) and \(\sin\delta \approx \delta\).

Sum of Longitudinal Forces: \[\sum F_{x,cg} = F_{x1} - F_{y1}\delta + F_{x2}\] Explanation: The total longitudinal force. Note that the front lateral tire force \(F_{y1}\) points slightly backward when steered by angle \(\delta\), creating a drag component.
Sum of Lateral Forces: \[\sum F_{y,cg} = F_{y1} + F_{y2}\] Explanation: The total lateral force is simply the sum of the lateral forces from the front and rear equivalent tires (ignoring the small longitudinal force component for small steering angles).
Sum of Yaw Moments: \[\sum M_{z,cg} = F_{y1}a - F_{y2}b\] Explanation: The turning moment around the CG, calculated by multiplying the lateral tire forces by their respective distances from the CG (\(a\) for front, \(b\) for rear).





These geometric relationships couple the vehicle’s rigid body velocities with the localized velocities at the tires.

Steady-State Yaw Rate: \[\omega_z = \frac{v_x}{R}\] Explanation: For steady-state cornering on a constant radius \(R\), the yaw rate is directly proportional to the forward speed.
Vehicle Side Slip Angle: \[\beta = -\frac{v_y}{v_x}\] Explanation: The angle between the vehicle’s longitudinal axis and its actual velocity vector at the center of gravity (assuming small angles where \(\tan\beta \approx \beta\)).
Front Tire Side Slip Angle (Linearized): \[\alpha_1 = \delta - \frac{v_y + a\omega_z}{v_x}\] Explanation: The side slip angle of the front tire. It is the difference between the steering angle (\(\delta\)) and the actual path angle of the front wheel (which is affected by both lateral velocity \(v_y\) and the yawing motion \(a\omega_z\)).
Rear Tire Side Slip Angle (Linearized): \[\alpha_2 = -\frac{v_y - b\omega_z}{v_x}\] Explanation: The side slip angle of the rear tire. It is similar to the front, but there is no steering angle (\(\delta = 0\)), and the yaw effect opposes the lateral velocity (hence the \(- b\omega_z\)).





To close the loop, you must link the kinematic slip angles to the dynamic forces.

Lateral Tire Force: \[F_{yi} = C_{F\alpha i}\alpha_i\] Explanation: The linear tire model assumes that for small slip angles, the lateral force generated by tire \(i\) is directly proportional to its slip angle \(\alpha_i\), scaled by the tire’s cornering stiffness \(C_{F\alpha i}\).

title: Control
text:
We can reconstruct the target velocity using: \[
v_{target} = v_i + \dot{d_i}
\]
This cannot be done for the acceleration of the target. That is why it uses a kalman filter (state observer) to estimate the accelration. This is based on the following assumptions: - between the samples which are taken with \(T_s\) the acceleration is assumed to be constant - any real changes in acceleration are treated as process white noise \(w_k\) acting on the system. Sensor inaccuracies are represented by measurement white noise \(v_k\).
This results in the following equations.
State equation \[x_{k+1} = A x_k + B u_k + G w_k\]
Measurement equation \[y_k = C x_k + D u_k + v_k\]
With \[
x_k = \begin{bmatrix} d_i \\ v_{target} \\ a_{target} \end{bmatrix} \qquad
A_k = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & T_s & \frac{T_s^2}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & T_s \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \qquad
u_k = \begin{bmatrix} v_i \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \qquad
y_k = \begin{bmatrix} d_i \\ \dot{d}_i \end{bmatrix}
\]
State estimate is then:
\[\tilde{x}_{k+1} = A\tilde{x}_k + Bu_k + L(y_k - C\tilde{x}_k - Du_k)\]
This now results in various delays. The first delay is due to the kalman filter. Afterwards it takes time to apply the brakes. To mitigate the delays we can predict where the vehicle will be in \(\Delta t\) seconds in the future.
Prediction of host velocity \[\bar{v}_i = v_i + \Delta t a_i\]
Prediction of target velocity \[\bar{v}_t = v_t + \Delta t a_t\]
Prediction range \[\bar{d}_i = \tilde{d}_i + (v_t - v_i)\Delta t + \frac{(a_t - a_i)\Delta t^2}{2}\]
Relative velocity: \[(v_t - v_i) + (a_t - a_i)t_f = 0\]
This gives us \[t_f = -\frac{v_t - v_i}{a_t - a_i}\]
Relative distance: \[d_i + (v_t - v_i)t_f + \frac{(a_t - a_i)t_f^2}{2} = 0\]
Filling \(t_1\) gives us the required host acceleration \[a_i = a_t - \frac{(v_t - v_i)^2}{2d_i}\]



image.png





image.png





The desired vehcile following distance is \(d_r = r + h \cdot v_i\), in which $h# is the headway time. Typically \(d_i>d_r\) for safety. For comfort you want to limit \(a_i\) and \(\dot{a_i}\) and it must also satisfy speed limits therefore \(v_i \le v_{max}\)
so we need a vehicle model which takes int o account: - drive force (non-linear) - Aerodynamic drag (quadratic with speed) \[
\begin{aligned}
F_{air} &= \frac{1}{2}\rho c_wA(v_x-v_w)^2\\
\rho &\approx 1.25 kg/m^3\\
c_wA &\approx 0.64 m^2 \\
\end{aligned}
\] - Rolling resistance (constant) and drag forces \[
\begin{aligned}
F_r &= f_rmg + k_{lin}v_x\\
f_r &\approx 0.0125\\
k_{lin} &\approx 2. Ns/m\\
\end{aligned}
\]
The total force equation therefore becomes: \[
\begin{aligned}
m_{eff} a_x = & -mgf_r - k_{lin}v_x \\
& - \frac{1}{2}\rho c_w A(v_x - v_w)^2
\end{aligned}
\] In what \(m_{eff}\) is the effective mass of the car. However what is actually \(m_{eff}\)? \[
\begin{aligned}
E_{kin} &= \frac{1}{2}mv_x^2 + \frac{4}{2}I_w \omega_w^2 + i^2 I_{motor}\omega_w^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\underbrace{\left( m + \frac{4I_w}{r_w^2} + \frac{i^2 I_{motor}}{r_w^2} \right)}_{m_{eff}} v_x^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{2}m_{eff} v_x^2
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Perception
text:
This contains only the notes that was mentioned that should be studied. However the levels of automated driving is also added.  Also just to be sure some types of sensors. 


Classification: - Determine class of the object within its general category
Detection: - Find the location of objects from a general category in sensor data
Ranging: - Estimate distance of a detected object
Recognition: - Find exactly the same object instance in sensor data
Tracking: - Estimate (and predict) path of a detected object - Recognition over time





precision is the percentage of correct detections. \[
Prec = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}
\]



Recall is the percentage of how many of the postives it could find out of the dataset \[
Rec= \frac{TP}{TP + FN}
\]



The F1-score is a trade off between precision and recall \[
F_1 = \frac{2}{\frac{1}{Rec}+\frac{1}{Prec}}= \frac{2*Rec*Prec}{Rec+Prec} = \frac{2|TP|}{2|TP|+|FP|+|FN|}
\]

Lecture 3 Introduction to deep learning
When the feature computation and classifier are designed manually this is also called model-based. Which has various problems like occlusions, lighting etc. In deep learning the feature computation and the classifier are trained. It is now data-driven
Some activation functions are given below:



image.png


The binary cross entropy loss is given by: \[
\lambda = y \cdot log(f(x)) + (1-y) \cdot log(1-f(x))
\]
Overfitting can be reduced by using L2 Regularization (Frobenius norm), this just the same as ridge idk why it is called like that. 
Methods to reduce overfitting are: - Dropout - Regularization - Early stopping

section: Lecture 4 Limitations of datasets & object detection
text:
Lecture 4 Limitations of datasets & object detection
Any dataset always represents a limited view on / only a sample of on the real world and therefore hard to generalize. Therefore partly data augmentation exists, one of these is shearing in which you hold the axis perpendiculr but place the corner of the image in a different position. This way you simulate camera angles and such.
The pooling operation has the following results: - Promotes dominat features - introduces translational invariance -Suppresses noise - reduces dimensionality
The softmax function is given as: \[
softmax(y)=\frac{e^y}{\sum e^y}
\]
In detection you want to have the follwing output vector: 
However it is difficult to predict: - different absolute positsions of objects - different shapes (aspect ratio) of objects that may also overlay
Therefore it is easier to predict an offset in position and size relative to a predefined, reference bounding (anchor) box. So you get:



image.png


Mostly DNN networks contain 3 components: - region proposals - Network predictions using feature extraction - Non-maximum suppressions (cleaning up)



image.png





image.png





image.png



Evaluation metrics

IoU
Intersection over union. \[
\text{IoU}(B_P, B_{GT}) = J(B_P, B_{GT}) = \frac{|B_P \cap B_{GT}|}{|B_P \cup B_{GT}|}
\]
Where: * \(B_P\): Predicted Bounding Box * \(B_{GT}\): Ground Truth Bounding Box * \(B_P \cap B_{GT}\): Area of Overlap (Intersection) * \(B_P \cup B_{GT}\): Area of Encompassed Region (Union)


Average precision
this is the area under the precision-recall curve. \[AP = \int_{r=0}^{1} p(r) \, dr\] in which p(r) is based on the confidence threshold


Mean average precision
This is the same as the average precision but now the mean is taken over the classes \[
mAP= \frac{1}{K}= \sum^K_{c=1}AP(c)
\]
You can calculate the mAP for different levels of IoU threshold. Then we get e.g. mAP@0.5, mAP@0.75, which is also noted as \(AP_{50}\). Sometimes mAP is reported as the mean of mAP over different IoU thresholds. mAP@[.50:.95] or mAP@[.50:.05:.95]

title: Perception
text:
Lecture 5 Object detection with lidar
3D data has other challengens: - Amount of data is much higher therefore real-time processing is more demanding - 3D point cloud data is irregular/ non-uniform / unstructured - No fixed grid compared to 2D grid of pixels i images -> point \(n\) can be anywhere in 3D space - Occlusions (objects cast ‘shadow’)
the 3d data can be represented using: - point-based - voxel-based - pillar-based (basically voxel-based except that each pillar does have unlimited height) - Graph-based - projection-based (Front view or also called range view) - projection-based (Birds eye view)

Data representations overview

Point-based
Keeps unstructured form however is often down-sampled to a fixed size of N points.


Voxel-based
The 3d space is partitioned into voxels, points are assigned to voxels. It can be done in 3 ways: - fixed voxelization - dynamic voxelization - hybrid scale voxelization (uses various sizes of voxels)



image.png




Projection based (Front view - Spherical)
Basically what you do is that you map a point from x,y,z into speherical coordinate representation and then unroll this sphere into a 2d map. The radar is supposed to be the middle of the sphere. 
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Azimuth } \phi_i &= arctan(\frac{y_i}{x_i})\\
\text{Polar / elevation } \theta_i &= arccos(\frac{z_i}{r_i})\\
\text{radial distance } r_i &= \sqrt{x_i^2 + y_i^2 + z_i^2}
\end{aligned}
\]


Projection based (cylindrical)
Is basically the same but now the coordinates are in cylindrical instead of spherical.


Projection birds eye view
The points are mapped into 2d with grid size \(\lambda\)
